propositions.text: Appellant is a Mexican citizen appealing RPD decision denying refugee protection due to internal flight alternative in Merida.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Andres or Appellant) is a citizen of Mexico. He is appealing a Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision that found he was not entitled to refugee protection on the grounds that he had an internal flight alternative (IFA)-a place where he would be safe and where it would be reasonable for him to relocate to-in Merida, Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant is a Mexican citizen appealing an RPD decision denying refugee protection due to an internal flight alternative in Merida.

propositions.text: Appellant argues RPD erred in finding he would be safe in Merida.
propositions.quote: On this appeal, XXXX makes various arguments to the effect that the RPD erred in finding that he will be safe in Merida.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD erred in finding he would be safe in Merida.

propositions.text: Not persuaded by appellant's arguments; appellant has not shown he lacks an IFA in Merida and is not entitled to refugee protection.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded by XXXX arguments that the RPD erred in its decision. XXXX has not established that he does not have an IFA in Merida. He is therefore not entitled to refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court is not persuaded by the appellant's arguments and finds he has not established lack of an IFA in Merida, denying refugee protection.

propositions.text: Appeal is dismissed; RPD correctly found appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, agreeing with the RPD that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.

propositions.text: RPD summarized appellant's allegations about cartel threats, extortion, brother's murder, and related events in Mexico.
propositions.quote: XXXX has not taken issue with the RPD's summary of his allegations, as follows:2 [8] The claimant, who is now XXXX years old alleges fear from a Mexican cartel which he believes to be the Familia Michoacana. It started back in XXXX 2015 when he and his brother XXXX were working at his father's store in Tlalnepantla, near Mexico City and two unknown men came into the store and handed them a cell phone. Later that day they received a phone call telling them to hand over XXXX XXXX XXXX pesos if they didn't want something to happen to them. [9] The claimant and his brother decided to throw away the cell phone; the men returned and the claimant and his brother told them they did not have the money. Their father shut down the store for about 10 days. Nothing further happened with respect to this specific threat. [10] On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, the claimant and his brother, XXXX XXXX were celebrating a birthday of one of their cousins at the house of the claimant's parents in Tlalnepantla. XXXX and his wife were leaving to go see a friend, when just as he got outside he was shot in the back five times by a person the claimant believes to be affiliated with the cartel and who goes by the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX was taken to the hospital where he died shortly after. [11] The claimant believes his brother's death and the extortion attempt at the family store are related in part because they were relatively close in time and in part because of the rumours that he had heard about the cartel being involved and XXXX connection to the cartel. He also indicated that his brother had applied to be a police officer but had been overheard telling people that the Quinientos Cartel, which he believes is affiliated with the Familia Michoacana, was investing money in the campaign of the mayor at the time. The claimant alleges that this was also part of the reason for his brother's killing. [12] The claimant took his wife and children to stay in Veracruz for about one and a half to two months to live with his aunt because he believed he was in danger. While in Veracruz, the claimant's aunt heard that four men in a car were said to be asking about the claimant. [13] She felt could no longer house the claimant because of that so the claimant went back to Mexico State, to Vallejo (which is also a neighbourhood in Mexico City), and lived with his in-laws. He says he locked himself in for about six months. [14] After that period of time, things were quiet and the claimant went back to work in Tlalnepantla. [15] The claimant did not report the killing to the police despite claiming to know who the killer was. When asked why, the claimant said he didn't see the point because the police protect "them." The authorities did show up at his parents' house but as far as an investigation into his brother's killing the claimant said there wasn't one. [16] The claimant was able to go about his daily life without incident for approximately two years until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 when the claiman

paragraphs.summary: The RPD summarized the appellant's allegations about cartel threats, extortion, and his brother's murder in Mexico.

propositions.text: Appellant submitted new evidence: Yucatan Times article, CBC News article, and a letter with WhatsApp message and translation.
propositions.quote: XXXX has submitted and requested that the following documents be accepted as new evidence for this appeal: a. A Yucatan Times article entitled, "The renowned Mayan activist, Pedro Uc, was threatened with death in Yucatan; the alleged hit men also threatened to kill his family" (with a date of January 12, 2020, referenced at the end of the article), submitted with the Appellant's Record on January 21, 2020;3 b. A CBC News article entitled, "Homicide charge laid in stabbing death of Canadian man in Mexico", last updated April 23, 2019 (printed January 12, 2020), submitted with the Appellant's Record on January 21, 2020;4 and, c. A letter from XXXX representative dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020, along with a WhatsApp Message and English transcript of same, all of which was submitted on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant submitted new evidence including two news articles and a letter with WhatsApp message for the appeal.

propositions.text: The court will not admit the new evidence submitted by the appellant.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I am not admitting this evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court refuses to admit the new evidence submitted by the appellant.

propositions.text: IRPA allows new evidence on appeal only if it arose after RPD decision, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been brought before RPD.
propositions.quote: The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)5 anticipates that an appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) will ordinarily be based on the record of the RPD proceeding. According to the law,6 I can only accept new evidence on this appeal that: i. arose after the RPD decision (the RPD hearing took place on November 7, 2019, and the RPD issued its decision on November 26, 2019); ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD decision; or, iii. that XXXX could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before its decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA limits new evidence on appeal to evidence arising after RPD decision, not reasonably available before, or not reasonably expected to be brought before RPD.

propositions.text: If new evidence meets criteria, court must decide if it is new, credible, and relevant before acceptance.
propositions.quote: If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.7

paragraphs.summary: The court must assess if new evidence is new, credible, and relevant before accepting it if it meets criteria.

propositions.text: RAD Rules require application and criteria for new evidence acceptance, considering relevance, probative value, and availability.
propositions.quote: As provided under Rules 29 and 37 of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules),8 a person who does not provide a document or written submissions with their Appellant's Record must not use the document unless allowed by the RAD. A person must make an application in accordance with RAD Rule 37, and, must show that the documents meet the criteria for acceptance of new evidence under section 110(4) of the IRPA. In deciding the application, the RAD must consider any relevant factors, including the document's relevance and probative value, any new evidence the document brings to the appeal, and whether the person who is the subject of the appeal, with reasonable effort, could have provided the document or written submissions with their record.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RAD Rules require application and criteria for new evidence acceptance, including relevance and availability.

propositions.text: Yucatan Times article rejected as new evidence due to lack of submissions and unclear date relevance.
propositions.quote: The Yucatan Times article is rejected as new evidence because XXXX has not provided any submissions with respect to how this document meets the requirements set out in section 110(4) of the IRPA. I acknowledge that there is a date of January 12, 2020 at the end of the article, but there is no indication whether this is the date of the article or the date that it was printed. The date of January 12, 2020 is the same date that the CBC News article was printed, so it may well be referencing the date that the Yucatan Times article was printed. If it was the date of the article, then I would expect it to appear at the top of the article, as is the consistent practice of other news articles. All of this is to point out that it is not clear, and I have no submissions to explain whether this document arose after the RPD decision; was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD decision; or, that XXXX could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before its decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the Yucatan Times article as new evidence due to lack of submissions and unclear timing.

propositions.text: CBC News article rejected as new evidence because it predates RPD decision and was reasonably available.
propositions.quote: The CBC News article is rejected as new evidence because I have not been provided any submissions to explain how this article meets the requirements of section 110(4) of the IRPA. The header information on the printout of this article indicates that XXXX printed it out on January 12, 2020. However, the relevant date I must consider is the date of the article referenced at the beginning of the article, as is common with news articles, and that date is April 23, 2019. This article did not arise after the RPD decision, but instead arose well before the RPD decision. As the article is from CBC News, a public website, I can see no reasons why this was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD decision; or, that XXXX could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before its decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the CBC News article as new evidence because it predates the RPD decision and was reasonably available.

propositions.text: Representative's letter and WhatsApp message rejected as new evidence due to procedural non-compliance, lack of relevance, and vague timing.
propositions.quote: The representative's letter and WhatsApp message and translation are rejected as new evidence. These documents were filed after the Appellant's Record. XXXX has not complied with the requirements of Rules 29 and 37. The letter of February 1, 2020, from his representative does not constitute an affidavit or statutory declaration, as referenced in Rule 37(4). It is odd that the representative is providing evidence (i.e., describing what happened to XXXX XXXX by way of the letter of February 1, 2020, rather than XXXX himself providing that evidence. With respect to the criteria in Rule 29(4), I do not find this WhatsApp message relevant or probative. The English translation of the message indicates, "Now you are fucked, you and your family we got to know that you have been talking if anything happens to our organization we are going to kill them all watch out when you get back." I do not find this message relevant or probative because there is no indication who sent the message. There is no indication concerning the identity of the "organization" referenced. There is no indication that the sender has the motivation or ability to track XXXX to the proposed IFA. The evidence does not bring anything new to the appeal. The threat is so vague that it does not bring any new evidence to the appeal, in terms of whether XXXX faces any likelihood of harm in the proposed IFA. It is unclear whether XXXX with reasonable effort could have provided the message with his Appellant's Record. There is a date on the message of "XXXX XXXX" but no reference to the year. The representative's letter which accompanies the message does not provide a year of when the referenced events took place (the letter is dated February 1, 2020, but the events described in the letter do not reference a year). Again, the letter is not sworn evidence, and in any event, the timing of the events described in the letter is vague. For example, the letter states that XXXX came to the see the representative demanding help, but does not indicate when XXXX came to see her. The letter also indicates that XXXX family members have been "recently" contacted, but provides no specific date. The letter discusses XXXX interaction with his roommates, but provides no specific dates for these events.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the representative's letter and WhatsApp message as new evidence due to procedural non-compliance, lack of relevance, and vague timing.

propositions.text: Without admitting new evidence, court cannot order a new hearing under IRPA section 110(6).
propositions.quote: Having not admitted any documents under section 110(4) of IRPA, I am unable to order a new hearing under section 110(6) of IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court cannot order a new hearing as no new evidence was admitted under IRPA section 110(4).

propositions.text: Appellant failed to prove he lacks an IFA in Merida; court not persuaded by his arguments that RPD erred.
propositions.quote: XXXX has failed to meet the burden of establishing that he does not have an IFA in Merida. For the following reasons, I am not persuaded by his arguments that the RPD erred in its decision that XXXX has an IFA in Merida.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant failed to prove he lacks an IFA in Merida and is not persuaded the RPD erred.

propositions.text: Two-prong test for IFA: no serious persecution risk and it is not objectively unreasonable to relocate there.
propositions.quote: There is a two-prong test to determine whether there is an IFA.9 In order to find that XXXX has an IFA in Merida, first I must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of him being persecuted (section 96 of the IRPA), or that he would not be personally subjected to a danger described in paragraph 97(1)(a), or to a risk described in paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA, in the proposed IFA. Second, I must determine that in all of the circumstances, including the circumstances particular to XXXX, conditions in the part of the country where a potential IFA has been identified are such that it would not be objectively unreasonable for him to seek refuge there before seeking protection in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the two-prong test for IFA: no serious persecution risk and reasonable to relocate there.

propositions.text: RPD gave notice to appellant that Merida was proposed as IFA; burden then on appellant to prove otherwise.
propositions.quote: The RPD member correctly gave notice to XXXX at the RPD hearing that Merida was being proposed as an IFA.10 After providing such notice, the burden of proof with respect to the two-prong IFA test then rested with XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD gave notice that Merida was proposed as IFA and burden shifted to appellant to prove otherwise.

propositions.text: Appellant's submissions focus on first prong of IFA test: no serious persecution risk in Merida.
propositions.quote: On this appeal, XXXX submissions as to why he believes the RPD erred in its decision centre around the first prong of the IFA test (i.e., whether, on a balance of probabilities, there is no serious possibility of him being persecuted in Merida (section 96 of the IRPA), or that he would not be personally subjected to a danger described in paragraph 97(1)(a), or to a risk described in paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD erred on the first prong of the IFA test regarding persecution risk in Merida.

propositions.text: RPD found no link between alleged risk and Convention grounds of persecution.
propositions.quote: The RPD member noted that based on the evidence, she was unable to find that the alleged risk XXXX faces in Mexico has a link to any of the Convention grounds of race, religion, nationality, particular social group, or political opinion.

propositions.text: Appellant argues cartel threat links to Convention grounds of particular social group persecution.
propositions.quote: XXXX argues that, "The evidence presented to the RPD by The Appellant clearly shows that The Cartel In Mexico has link to The Convention grounds of a Particular group persecution (a threat to life or freedom)".

propositions.text: Court rejects appellant's argument; appellant must prove link to Convention grounds and serious persecution risk, which he has not.
propositions.quote: I do not accept XXXX argument for the following reasons. XXXX must establish that he falls into one of the Convention grounds referred to in section 96 of the IRPA, and that there would be a serious possibility of persecution of him by reason of such Convention ground in the proposed IFA of Merida. He has not shown this, and the evidence does not support it.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no link between risk and Convention grounds; appellant argues there is such a link; court rejects appellant's argument for lack of proof.

propositions.text: RPD found appellant did not know who tried to extort him or his brother's killer; evidence based on rumor.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that with respect to the safety of the IFA, XXXX does not know who tried to extort him and his brother. The RPD indicated that XXXX said the killer of his brother was a person named XXXX, and he believes the agents of harm might be part of the Michoacana cartel, but was only basing that on rumour.

propositions.text: RPD found appellant did not establish that those involved in extortion or murder would travel to Veracruz to harm him.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that XXXX had not sufficiently established that those who were involved in the extortion attempt and/or his brother's murder were willing and able to travel to Veracruz, where XXXX had been for a period of time, to locate him, let alone harm him.

propositions.text: RPD found appellant had fearful incidents but did not know or only speculated about perpetrators based on rumor.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that while XXXX may have had fearful incidents, including the tragic death of his brother, when he was asked who these people were, XXXX did not know or speculated who they were based on rumour.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found appellant did not know who extorted or killed his brother and had only rumors; no proof they would harm him in Veracruz.

propositions.text: It is speculative that he would not be subjected to risk of harm in the IFA and no real evidence shows absence of risk
propositions.quote: XXXX argues that it is speculative that he would not be subjected to a risk of harm, and he submits that there is no real evidence that the risk mentioned would not be present.

propositions.text: There is no guarantee of absence of risk and the IFA would increase risk to his entire family
propositions.quote: XXXX submits that there is not a guarantee of the absence of risk, and that the IFA would increase the risk to his entire family.

propositions.text: Organized crime networks leave hardly any visible traces or evidence
propositions.quote: XXXX argues that organized crime networks hardly leave any visible traces or evidence.

propositions.text: He is a victim of organized crime without proof of the organization's identity, which is the Mexican authorities' obligation
propositions.quote: XXXX argues that he is a victim of organized crime and does not carry proof of the identity of the organization. He argues that identification is the obligation of the Mexican authorities, and to pursue clarifying the identification of those responsible for his brother's death would incite and increase the actual risk.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues risk of harm in IFA is speculative, no proof of absence of risk, risk to family increased, organized crime leaves no evidence, and ID is authorities' duty.

propositions.text: Does not accept applicant's arguments for reasons explained
propositions.quote: I do not accept XXXX arguments for the following reasons.

propositions.text: It is applicant's burden to establish likelihood of harm in the proposed IFA, not RPD's or RAD's to prove absence of risk
propositions.quote: It is not the RPD's or the RAD's responsibility to refer to evidence that guarantees an absence of risk in the proposed IFA. Rather, as stated at the outset of this section, it is XXXX burden to establish that there is the requisite likelihood of harm in the proposed IFA.

propositions.text: Applicant lacks proof of identity of harm agents and says proving identity is Mexican authorities' obligation
propositions.quote: XXXX argues that he does not have proof of the identity of the organization, and that proving identity is the obligation of the Mexican authorities.

propositions.text: Applicant's speculation on agents of harm and their motivation/ability to pursue him in Merida is insufficient to meet risk standard
propositions.quote: However, this leaves XXXX with only his speculation as to the agents of harm, and also speculation whether they have the motivation and ability to pursue him in the IFA of Merida. Speculation is insufficient to meet the required standard of there being a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk of section 97(1) harm in Merida.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects applicant's arguments, stating burden is on applicant to prove harm likelihood; speculation insufficient to meet risk standard.

propositions.text: RPD found little credible evidence that applicant's profile interests agents of harm; first prong of IFA test not met
propositions.quote: The RPD member decided that there was little, if any, credible evidence that XXXX profile would be of interest to the agents of harm, and that the first prong of the IFA test had not been met.

propositions.text: Applicant argues insufficient evidence that agents of harm would not pursue him or family to Merida
propositions.quote: XXXX argues that there is insufficient evidence that the agent of harm would not be interested in pursuing him to Merida or to his entire family.

propositions.text: Does not accept applicant's argument and explains burden is on applicant to prove risk in IFA, not on RPD to prove absence
propositions.quote: I do not accept XXXX argument for the following reasons. First, XXXX is attempting to reverse the burden. Once an IFA is proposed, it is XXXX burden to establish that he faces a serious possibility of persecution, or on a balance of probabilities, a section 97(1) risk in the IFA. It is not the RPD's burden to establish that he would not face such a risk.

propositions.text: Applicant has not established serious possibility of persecution or risk in Merida IFA
propositions.quote: XXXX has not established that he faces a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a section 97(1) risk in the IFA of Merida.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted CNN article indicating La Familia Michoacana is possibly defunct and active only in other states, not Yucatan where Merida is
propositions.quote: In fact, XXXX submitted an article from CNN to the RPD entitled, "Mexico Drug War Facts", updated August 27, 2019, that indicates that La Familia Michoacana (the organization that XXXX speculates is the alleged agent of harm) is "Based in the Michoacan state. Possibly defunct as of 2011. It announced it would disband in 2010, but some cells are still active in Guerrero and Mexico states, according to the Congressional Research Service report." The proposed IFA of Merida is not in Michoacan, Guerrero or Mexico state, but is instead located farther away in Yucatan state.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found little evidence applicant's profile interests harm agents; court rejects applicant's burden-reversal argument and notes CNN article on cartel's limited presence.

propositions.text: RPD found after six months hiding, things were quiet and applicant returned to work in fall 2016; noise triggering flight was in 2018
propositions.quote: The RPD member decided that after six months of hiding, things were quiet and XXXX went back to work in the fall of 2016. The RPD noted that the noise that XXXX heard, which triggered his flight from Mexico, happened almost two years later in XXXX 2018.

propositions.text: RPD found no incidents before 2018 noise and applicant does not know who caused commotion
propositions.quote: The RPD indicated that there were no incidents leading up to that time, and that XXXX does not know who caused the commotion he heard at his parents' place that caused him to flee.

propositions.text: Applicant argues no incidents because he escaped and reached safe destination
propositions.quote: XXXX argues that there were no incidents because he escaped and ran for his life, and made it to a safe destiny.

propositions.text: Does not accept applicant's argument; noise source unknown and speculation about threats insufficient; applicant left hiding in 2016 and lived incident-free until 2018 noise
propositions.quote: I do not accept XXXX argument for the following reasons. First, XXXX is speculating that the noise he heard was someone coming to harm him. He does not know the source of the noise he heard in XXXX 2018, and he is speculating when he suggests he did not receive any threats prior to then because he was in hiding. As noted by the RPD, he had left hiding to go back to work in the XXXX of 2016. He then went about his daily life without incident until he heard a loud noise in XXXX 2018.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found applicant returned to work in 2016 and no incidents before 2018 noise; applicant argues no incidents due to escape; court rejects speculation.

propositions.text: RPD reviewed National Documentation Package (NDP) for Mexico and noted info about Mexico and Merida IFA
propositions.quote: The RPD member indicated in her decision that she reviewed the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Mexico, and noted information about Mexico and the proposed IFA of Merida.

propositions.text: Applicant argues NDP might be outdated and needs review
propositions.quote: XXXX argues that the NDP for Mexico might not be up to date and needs to be reviewed.

propositions.text: Does not accept applicant's argument; no submissions or info provided to show specific NDP info cited by RPD is in error
propositions.quote: I do not accept XXXX' argument for the following reasons. First, he has not provided any submissions why he believes any of the specific information cited by the RPD is in error. Second, he has not provided any information of his own, either other studies or articles included in the NDP or not included in the NDP, that demonstrates how any of the specific information cited by the RPD is in error.

paragraphs.summary: RPD reviewed NDP on Mexico and Merida; applicant argues NDP outdated; court rejects argument for lack of evidence.

propositions.text: RPD noted Familia Michoacana is reducing in power and has no presence in Merida IFA
propositions.quote: The RPD member referred to information in the NDP that indicates that Familia Michoacana is reducing in power and that the cartel does not have a presence in the IFA.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Familia Michoacana leader might be replaced by another
propositions.quote: XXXX argues that the Familia Michoacan leader might be replaced by another one.

propositions.text: Does not accept applicant's speculation about new leader and cartel presence; decision must be based on evidence not speculation
propositions.quote: I do not accept XXXX argument for the following reasons. First, he is speculating that there might be a new leader. Second, he is speculating that if there is a new leader it would mean that the cartel would then develop a presence in the IFA of Merida. I must base a decision on evidence, not speculation.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found cartel declining and absent in Merida; applicant speculates on new leader; court rejects speculation, requires evidence.

propositions.text: Dismisses appeal and confirms RPD decision that appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses appeal and confirms RPD decision denying refugee protection.
